extracted.intended_audience: editors, publishers, authors, peer reviewers, and staff of peer-reviewed medical/biomedical journals
extracted.subtask_short: journal COI policy for medical journals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for creating, declaring, and managing conflicts of interest policies for peer-reviewed medical journals, covering authors, peer reviewers, and editors. Emphasizes disclosure, scope (financial and non-financial), management actions, and transparency practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and scope
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear definition the journal uses as to what is conflict of interest and who is captured in the definition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sample definition given: "conflict of interest exists when a participant in the publication process (author, peer reviewer or editor) has a competing interest that could unduly influence (or be reasonably seen to do so) his or her responsibilities in the publication process (submission of manuscripts, peer review, editorial decisions, and communication between authors, reviewers and editors)."

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of competing interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement of examples of the types of competing interests (and their definitions) the journal says must be declared.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: WAME lists examples that should be included (but is not limited to): (I) Financial ties; (II) Academic commitments; (III) Personal relationships; (IV) Political or religious beliefs; (V) Institutional affiliations. Guidance notes the need to consider a wide range of competing interests, recognize they can coexist, and move beyond focusing only on financial conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Declaring conflict of interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Clear statements on what is to be declared, when and to whom, the format for declaration, the journal’s role in asking additional questions or seeking clarification about disclosures, and consequences for failing to disclose before or after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals rely on declarants because routine monitoring is not possible; therefore the policy should make clear what to declare, require comprehensive reporting, specify format and timing, and explain how the journal will follow up or seek clarification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Managing conflict of interests
rubrics_metrics.description: A clear statement on how conflict of interest will be managed by the journal, including which disclosures will be published and what conflict situations will result in a manuscript not being considered.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should state the journal's approach (which may vary across journals), clarify which conflicts lead to rejection or other actions, and make known how disclosures will affect editorial decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication/Transparency of disclosures
rubrics_metrics.description: All relevant conflict of interest disclosures (or the declaration of no conflict of interest) will be published with the article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers require transparency; editors should publish relevant author disclosures with every article so readers have uncensored information to judge potential influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expanded scope beyond financial conflicts
rubrics_metrics.description: Extend the concept of financial conflict of interest to include clinical income and non-financial conflicts such as scholarly commitment ("intellectual passion"), personal relationships, political or religious beliefs, and institutional affiliations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: physicians earning income from clinical services may be biased toward related technologies; intellectual commitments can bias judgement; personal and institutional loyalties can affect evaluation. Journals should articulate examples and definitions and move beyond only financial COI.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allow journals latitude in operational standards
rubrics_metrics.description: WAME does not prescribe a universal standard for when meaningful conflict exists and recommends elements of COI policies while leaving operational definitions and standards to individual journals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognizes global variation in context and evolving standards; offers factors to consider but encourages journals to set standards appropriate to their discipline and culture to avoid paralyzing peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' responsibility to investigate and act on failures to disclose
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors have a responsibility for investigating, and if relevant acting, if competing interests surface after a manuscript is submitted or published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose is serious; allegations must be taken seriously and may require investigation, corrective action, and possible sanctions (e.g., correction, retraction, editorial action).

rubrics_metrics.name: COI policies must cover all participants (authors, reviewers, editors)
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement addresses conflicts of interest threatening all participants in the research and publication continuum, including authors, peer reviewers, and editors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Also note conflicts between editors and journal owners are a distinct concern addressed in a separate WAME policy; policies should encompass the whole publication process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Full written disclosure as the backbone of management
rubrics_metrics.description: Full written disclosure is the backbone of managing conflicts of interest; without it nothing else is possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disclosure is an imperfect remedy; even with disclosure, editors must judge whether a conflict is sufficient to impair objectivity. Policies should emphasize comprehensive, written declarations and provide guidance on how editors should assess impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make COI policies readily accessible
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should make these policies readily accessible to everyone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should be published and available to authors, reviewers, editors and readers to ensure transparency and consistent application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design disclosure processes to maximize reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Journals should ask about conflict of interest in such a way that there will be a high likelihood of reporting relevant conflict of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because routine monitoring is not feasible, the journal’s questions and forms should be structured to prompt comprehensive reporting; the onus is on declarants to report carefully and comprehensively.
